title: Unit 5a - Operator Overloading Title Slide
summary: Title slide for Unit 5a on Operator Overloading in CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp. Covers how to define custom operator behavior for user-defined classes.
main_text: This unit covers Operator Overloading in C++, which allows programmers to define custom behavior for operators like +, -, ==, and << when used with user-defined classes. The unit is part of CS103 and is taught by Mark Redekopp. Topics include function overloading review, global vs member operator functions, friend functions, ostream overloading, and implicit type conversion.
notes_text: Operator overloading is part of Unit 5 (Objects 2), building on the class fundamentals learned in Unit 3. Students should be comfortable with classes, member functions, and references before this unit.

title: Function Overloading Review
summary: Reviews function signatures: name plus number/type of arguments define uniqueness. Return type alone does not make a signature unique; const does for members.
main_text: What makes up a signature (uniqueness) of a function: the name, and the number and type of arguments. No two functions are allowed to have the same signature; the following 4 functions are unique and allowable: void f1(int); void f1(double, int); void f1(double); void f1(int, int);. We say that 'f1' is overloaded 4 times. Notes: Return type does NOT make signature unique -- int f1(); is considered the same as void f1();. For member functions, 'const' makes signature unique -- int& List::get() and int const & List::get() const are different signatures.
notes_text: Function overloading is a prerequisite concept for operator overloading. The key rule about return types not contributing to uniqueness is important -- students often incorrectly assume changing the return type creates a new overload. The const qualifier creating a unique signature for member functions is relevant for operator overloading where const correctness matters.

title: Operator Overloading Motivation
summary: Explains that C++ operators work with built-in types but not user-defined classes. Custom functions can define operator behavior for new classes.
main_text: C/C++ defines operators (+, *, -, ==, etc.) that work with basic data types like int, char, double, etc. C/C++ has no clue what classes we'll define and what those operators would mean for these 'yet-to-be-defined' classes. Examples: class complex { public: double real, imaginary; }; Complex c1, c2, c3; c3 = c1 + c2; // should add component-wise. class List { ... }; List l1, l2; l1 = l1 + l2; // should concatenate l2 items to l1. We can write custom functions to tell the compiler what to do when we use these operators! Let us learn how...
notes_text: This slide motivates the entire unit. The Complex number example is intuitive -- adding two complex numbers should add their real and imaginary parts separately. The List concatenation example shows operators can mean different things for different classes. The key insight: operators are just function calls with special syntax.

title: Two Approaches to Operator Overloading
summary: There are two ways to define operator overloads: as a global function or as a member function of the class. The choice depends on the left-hand side operand type.
main_text: There are two ways to specify an operator overload function: 1. Global level function (not a member of any class). 2. As a member function of the class on which it will operate. Which should we choose? It depends on the type of the left-hand side operand. Example 1: string + int -- the LHS is a string, so operator+ could be a member of the string class. Example 2: iostream << Location -- the LHS is an iostream, so operator<< would need to be related to iostream (but we can't modify iostream, so we use a friend function instead).
notes_text: This is the central design decision in operator overloading. The rule is simple: if the LHS is your class, use a member function. If the LHS is someone else's class (like ostream for <<), you must use a global/friend function. This distinction comes up repeatedly throughout the unit.

title: Method 1: Global Operator Functions
summary: Shows how to define global operator functions named 'operator{+-...}' taking two arguments (LHS as 1st, RHS as 2nd). Compiler matches and calls them automatically.
main_text: Can define global functions with name 'operator{+-...}' taking two arguments. LHS = Left Hand side is 1st arg, RHS = Right Hand side is 2nd arg. When compiler encounters an operator with objects of specific types it will look for an 'operator' function to match and call it. But what if we need to access private data of some object to implement our operation? A global (non-member) function will not work. We need method 2. Example: string operator+(int time, string suf) { string res = to_string(time); res += suf; return res; }. In main: int hour = 9; string suffix = "p.m."; string time = hour + suffix; // WILL COMPILE TO: string time = operator+(hour, suffix);
notes_text: The key insight is that 'hour + suffix' is syntactic sugar for 'operator+(hour, suffix)'. The compiler automatically translates operator expressions into function calls. The limitation of global functions is that they cannot access private members of classes, which motivates member functions and friend functions.

title: Method 2: Class Member Operator Functions
summary: Shows operator overloading as class member functions. The LHS is the implicit calling object, and the RHS is passed as the argument.
main_text: C++ allows users to write class member functions that define what an operator should do for a class. Same naming convention: function name starts with 'operator' and then the actual operator. Important: Left-hand side is the implied calling object for which the member function is called and Right-hand side is passed as the argument: LHS-arg.operator+(RHS-arg);. Example with Complex class: class Complex { public: Complex(); Complex(double r, double i); Complex operator+(const Complex &rhs) const; private: double real, imag; };. Implementation: Complex Complex::operator+(const Complex &rhs) const { Complex temp; temp.real = real + rhs.real; temp.imag = imag + rhs.imag; return temp; }. Usage: Complex c3 = c1 + c2; // Same as c3 = c1.operator+(c2);
notes_text: The member function approach is cleaner when the LHS is an instance of your class. Note the const qualifier on the function -- operator+ should not modify either operand. The RHS is passed by const reference for efficiency. The return type is Complex (by value) because we create a new result.

title: Overloading Notes - What Can and Cannot Be Overloaded
summary: Lists which operators can be overloaded (binary, comparison, assignment, I/O) and notes that precedence cannot be changed.
main_text: You can overload any operator except the member operator (.), the scope operator (::), and the ternary operator (?:). Binary operators: +, -, *, /, ++, --. Comparison operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=. Assignment: =, +=, -=, *=, /=, etc. I/O stream operators: <<, >>. You cannot change the operator's precedence -- multiply must always come before addition. More questions can be found at https://isocpp.org/wiki/faq/operator-overloading.
notes_text: The inability to change precedence is important. Even if you overload + and * for your class, the compiler still evaluates * before + in expressions like a + b * c. The list of non-overloadable operators is small but important to remember for exams.

title: Binary Operator Overloading - Return New Object
summary: For binary operators, create a new object with the result and return it. Do not modify the input operands. Order of operations and associativity still apply.
main_text: For binary operators, do the operation on a new object's data members and return that object. Don't want to affect the input operands' data members. There is a difference between: x = y + z; (creates new result, assigns to x) vs. x = x + z; (also creates new result, then assigns back to x). Normal order of operations and associativity apply (can't be changed). Can overload each operator with various RHS types -- see next slide.
notes_text: This is a critical design principle: binary operators like + should be non-mutating. They create and return a NEW object. This differs from compound assignment operators like += which DO modify the left operand. Students often make the mistake of modifying the calling object in operator+.

title: Binary Operator Overloading with Multiple Types and Chaining
summary: Shows overloading operator+ for Complex+Complex and Complex+int separately. Demonstrates that chaining (c1+c2+c3) works automatically via binary calls.
main_text: The Complex class declares two overloads: Complex operator+(const Complex &rhs) const; for adding two Complex numbers, and Complex operator+(int real) const; for adding a Complex and an int. Implementation for Complex+Complex: Complex temp; temp.real = real + rhs.real; temp.imag = imag + rhs.imag; return temp;. Implementation for Complex+int: Complex temp = *this; temp.real += real; return temp;. Chaining: Complex c4 = c1 + c2 + c3; compiles to c4 = c1.operator+(c2).operator+(c3) which becomes anonymous-ret-val.operator+(c3). No special code is needed to add 3 or more operands -- the compiler chains multiple calls to the binary operator in sequence. Adding different types (Complex + Complex vs. Complex + int) requires different overloads.
notes_text: The chaining mechanism is elegant: operator+ returns a Complex by value, and that temporary can immediately have operator+ called on it for the next operand. This is why the return type must be Complex (not void). The *this usage in the int overload copies the current object into temp before modifying it.

title: Relational Operator Overloading
summary: Shows how to overload comparison operators (==, !=, <, etc.) which should return bool. Example compares two Complex numbers for equality.
main_text: Can overload ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=. Should return bool. Example: class Complex declares bool operator==(const Complex &rhs) const;. Implementation: bool Complex::operator==(const Complex &rhs) const { return (real == rhs.real && imag == rhs.imag); }. Usage: Complex c1(2,3); Complex c2(4,5); if(c1 == c2) // equiv. to c1.operator==(c2); cout << "C1 & C2 are equal!" << endl;. Since c1 has (2,3) and c2 has (4,5), they are not equal, so nothing will be displayed.
notes_text: Relational operators return bool, not the class type. The operator== for Complex checks both real and imaginary parts. For floating-point comparisons in production code, you'd typically use an epsilon tolerance rather than exact equality, but this example uses exact comparison for simplicity.

title: Non-Member Functions - When LHS Is Not Your Class
summary: When the LHS is not an instance of your class (e.g., 5 + c1), member functions won't work. A non-member global function taking both operands is needed.
main_text: What if the user changes the order? If int is on LHS and Complex on RHS: Complex c3 = 5 + c1; This tries to call 5.operator+(c1) or int.operator+(c1), but there is no int class we can change or write. No match to a member function because to call a member function the LHS has to be an instance of that class. We can define a non-member function (global scope function) that takes in two parameters (both the LHS and RHS). May need to declare it as a friend. Example: Complex operator+(const int& lhs, const Complex &rhs) { Complex temp; temp.real = lhs + rhs.real; temp.imag = rhs.imag; return temp; }. Usage: Complex c3 = 5 + c1; // Calls operator+(5, c1). Still a problem: Can operator+(...) access Complex's private data?
notes_text: This slide reveals a fundamental limitation of member operator functions: they only work when the LHS is an instance of your class. For commutative operations like addition, you often need both a member function (Complex + int) and a non-member function (int + Complex). The private access problem motivates friend functions.

title: Friend Functions - Accessing Private Data from Non-Members
summary: A friend function is not a class member but has access to private data. Declared with 'friend' keyword in the class definition, without scope qualifier.
main_text: A friend function is a function that is not a member of the class but has access to the private data members of instances of that class. Put keyword 'friend' in function prototype in class definition. Don't add scope to function definition. Example: class Silly { public: Silly(int d) { dat = d }; friend int inc_my_data(Silly &s); private: int dat; };. The function is defined without Silly:: scope: int inc_my_data(Silly &a) { s.dat++; return s.dat; }. Notice inc_my_data is NOT a member function of Silly. It's a global scope function but now can access the private class members. In main: Silly cat(5); // cat.dat = 8 WON'T COMPILE since dat is private. int x = inc_my_data(cat); // works because inc_my_data is a friend.
notes_text: Friend functions break encapsulation selectively. They should be used sparingly -- primarily for operator overloading when the LHS is not your class. Key syntax rules: 'friend' keyword goes in the class declaration, but the function definition has no class scope (no Silly:: prefix).

title: Non-Member Friend Operator Function - Solution
summary: Shows the complete solution: declare operator+ as a friend in the Complex class, allowing it to access private real and imag for int + Complex operations.
main_text: Revisiting the previous problem of int + Complex. The Complex class declares: friend Complex operator+(const int&, const Complex&);. This is not a member function -- it's a friend declaration. The implementation: Complex operator+(const int& lhs, const Complex &rhs) { Complex temp; temp.real = lhs + rhs.real; temp.imag = rhs.imag; return temp; }. Usage: Complex c3 = 5 + c1; // Calls operator+(5, c1). Now things work! The friend declaration gives the global operator+ function access to Complex's private members real and imag, solving the access problem from the previous slide.
notes_text: This completes the pattern for commutative operators: member function for Complex + int, friend function for int + Complex. Note the function definition has no Complex:: scope prefix since it is a global function, not a member.

title: Why Friend Functions - cout << Problem
summary: Shows that cout << c1 for a Complex object fails because ostream has no operator<< for Complex. The compiler error shows no matching operator.
main_text: Can I do the following? cout << c1; // equiv. to cout.operator<<(c1);. No! The compiler generates an error: 'no match for operator<< in std::cout << c1'. The error lists candidates that ostream does support: operator<<(long int), operator<<(long unsigned int), operator<<(bool), operator<<(short int), etc. But none accept a Complex object. The class Complex has operator+ defined as a member, but no operator<< because << would need to be called on cout (an ostream), not on the Complex object.
notes_text: This slide reveals why friend functions are essential for I/O operators. The expression cout << c1 translates to cout.operator<<(c1), making cout (ostream) the LHS. We cannot add member functions to ostream, so we must use a non-member (friend) function.

title: Why Friend Functions - ostream Analysis
summary: Explains that cout is an ostream object, << is an operator, and since we cannot modify ostream to add our class, we must use friend functions.
main_text: cout is an object of type ostream. << is just an operator. But we call it with cout on the LHS which would make operator<< a member function of class ostream. The ostream class can't define these member functions to print out user defined classes because they haven't been created. Similarly, ostream class doesn't have access to private members of Complex. The code shows: cout << "c1 = " << c1; which translates to cout.operator<<("c1 = ").operator<<(c1);. Using global scope (friend) functions: operator<<(operator<<(cout, "c1 = "), c1);. The chaining works because each call returns the ostream reference.
notes_text: The chaining explanation is critical: cout << a << b works because operator<<(cout, a) returns a reference to cout, allowing the second << b to chain. If operator<< returned void, chaining would fail. This is why operator<< must return ostream&.

title: Ostream Operator Overloading Implementation
summary: Shows the complete implementation of operator<< as a friend function. LHS is ostream& (1st arg), RHS is const Complex& (2nd arg). Returns ostream& for chaining.
main_text: Can define operator functions as friend functions. LHS is 1st arg. RHS is 2nd arg. Use friend function so LHS can be different type but still access private data. Return the ostream& (i.e. os which is really cout) so you can chain calls to operator<< and because cout/os object has changed. Class declaration: friend ostream& operator<<(ostream&, const Complex &c);. Implementation: ostream& operator<<(ostream &os, const Complex &c) { os << c.real << "," << c.imag << "j"; return os; }. Usage: Complex c1(2,3), c2(4,5); cout << c1 << c2; // operator<<(operator<<(cout, c1), c2);
notes_text: Key design decisions: (1) Return ostream& to enable chaining. (2) Pass ostream by non-const reference since output operations modify its state. (3) Pass Complex by const reference since we only read it. (4) The friend declaration in the class gives access to private real and imag members.

title: Implicit Type Conversion Operators
summary: Shows how to define implicit type conversion operators like operator bool() and operator int() to allow objects to be used in boolean/integer contexts.
main_text: Would the following if condition make sense? Student s1; if(s1) { cout << "Hi" << endl; }. No! If statements want Boolean variables. But you've done things like this before: ifstream ifile(filename); while(ifile >> x) { ... }. Operator>> returns an ifstream&, and ifstream has an implicit type conversion operator. So how does ifstream do it? With an 'implicit type conversion operator overload'. Example: class Student { private: int id; double gpa; public: operator bool() { return gpa >= 2.0; } operator int() { return id; } };. Student::operator bool() specifies how to convert a Student to a bool. Student::operator int() specifies how to convert a Student to an int. Usage: Student s1; if(s1) // calls operator bool(). int x = s1; // calls operator int().
notes_text: Implicit conversion operators have no return type in their declaration (the return type is implied by the operator name). They also take no arguments since they convert 'this' object. The ifstream example is familiar to students from file I/O -- while(ifile >> x) works because ifstream converts to bool to indicate success/failure.

title: Member or Friend - Decision Flowchart
summary: Decision rule: if the LHS is an instance of your class C1, use a member function. If LHS is a different type, use a global (friend) function.
main_text: Should I make my operator overload be a member of a class, C1? Ask yourself: Is the LHS an instance of C1? YES: C1 objA; objA << objB // or objA + int. YES the operator overload function can be a member function of the C1 class since it will translate to objA.operator<<(...). NO: C1 objA; objB << objA // or int + objA. NO the operator overload function should be a global level (maybe friend) function such as operator<<(cout, objA). It cannot be a member function since it will translate to objB.operator<<(...) and objB is not of type C1.
notes_text: This is the key decision flowchart students should internalize. The green arrow (YES) path leads to member functions, the red arrow (NO) path leads to global/friend functions. The most common NO case is operator<< for output, where the LHS is always cout (an ostream).

images.description: Decision flowchart with YES/NO arrows: YES (green) leads to member function explanation, NO (red) leads to global/friend function explanation

title: Summary - Member vs Friend Functions
summary: If the LHS is an instance of that class, use a member function with one argument (RHS). If the LHS is a different class, use a friend function with two arguments.
main_text: If the left hand side of the operator is an instance of that class: Make the operator a member function of a class. The member function should only take in one argument which is the RHS object. If the left hand side of the operator is an instance of a different class: Make the operator a friend function of a class. This function requires two arguments, first is the LHS object and second is the RHS object.
notes_text: This summary crystallizes the two rules. Member functions: 1 argument (RHS), implicit this is LHS. Friend/global functions: 2 arguments (LHS then RHS). The argument count difference is because member functions have implicit access to the calling object via 'this'.

title: Operator Overloading Review Section Divider
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of review exercises for operator overloading concepts covered in this unit.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Operator Overloading Review section, which contains practice problems and review exercises to reinforce the concepts of member vs non-member operator functions, argument counts, return types, and chaining.
notes_text: The review section provides structured practice problems using a BigInt class example to test understanding of the key concepts.

title: Review: Member vs Non-Member and Arguments
summary: Review questions using BigInt class: when to use member vs non-member, and how many arguments member operator functions need for binary and unary operators.
main_text: Member or Non-member? How do you decide if you can make the operator overload function a member function of the class? When do you have to use a non-member operator function? Example: class BigInt { ... }; int main() { BigInt x, y, z; x = y + 5; }. Arguments: For member function operator overloads, how many input arguments are needed for operator+? For operator!? These are posed as questions for students to work through before seeing the solution.
notes_text: For x = y + 5: y is a BigInt (our class) on the LHS, so member function works. For operator+ as a member: 1 argument (the RHS). For operator! (unary): 0 arguments (only operates on this). These questions test the core concepts from the lecture.

title: Review: Return Types and Chaining
summary: Review questions on return types for operator+ (BigInt by value) and operator== (bool), plus whether multi-input overloads are needed for chaining.
main_text: Return types: For class BigInt which models an arbitrary precision integer, what should the return type be for Operator+? And for Operator==? Chaining: Do we need operator overload functions with 2-, 3-, 4-inputs, etc. to handle various use cases? Example: class BigInt { public: _______ operator+(const BigInt&); _______ operator==(const BigInt&); };. Usage: BigInt w, x, y, z; w = x + y; and w = x + y + z; cout << w << " is a bigint!" << endl;
notes_text: The answers: operator+ returns BigInt (by value, new object), operator== returns bool. No multi-argument overloads are needed -- chaining handles w = x + y + z via x.operator+(y).operator+(z). The return type of BigInt enables this chaining.

title: Solution Section Divider
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of solutions to the review questions posed in the previous slides.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the solutions section for the operator overloading review questions.
notes_text: Students should attempt the review questions before looking at the solutions.

title: Review Solutions: Member vs Non-Member and Arguments
summary: Answers: use member when LHS is class instance, non-member when LHS is not. operator+ needs 1 argument (RHS), operator! needs 0 (unary, 'this' is operand).
main_text: Member or Non-member? How do you decide if you can make the operator overload function a member function of the class? If the left-hand side operand is a class instance, you can use a member function. When do you have to use a non-member operator function? If the left operand of an operator is NOT an instance of the class, you cannot use a member function. Arguments: For member function operator overloads, how many input arguments are needed for operator+? Only 1, the left side operand is 'this'. For operator! (unary)? None, the left side operand is 'this'. Example: class BigInt { ____ operator+(const BigInt& rhs); ____ operator!(); };. Usage: w = x + y; // x.operator+(y). bool flag = !w; // w.operator!().
notes_text: The implicit 'this' pointer is the key to understanding argument counts. For member binary operators, 'this' is always the LHS, so only the RHS needs to be an explicit parameter. For unary operators like !, 'this' is the sole operand, so no explicit parameters are needed.

title: Review Solutions: Return Types and Chaining
summary: Answers: operator+ returns BigInt (by value), operator== returns bool. Chaining works automatically via x.operator+(y).operator+(z) -- no multi-arg overloads needed.
main_text: Return types: For class BigInt, operator+ should return BigInt (by value) and operator== should return bool. class BigInt { public: BigInt operator+(const BigInt&); bool operator==(const BigInt&); };. Chaining: Do we need operator overload functions with 2-, 3-, 4-inputs to handle various use cases? No, this is why the return type should be BigInt to allow for chaining: x.operator+(y).operator+(z), etc. Example: BigInt w, x, y, z; w = x + y + z; cout << w << " is a bigint!" << endl;. The expression x + y returns a temporary BigInt, then that temporary + z returns another BigInt, assigned to w.
notes_text: The return-by-value for operator+ is essential for chaining. If it returned void, w = x + y + z would fail. The bool return for operator== makes it usable in if-conditions naturally. For operator<<, the return is ostream& to enable chaining with cout.

title: Operator Overloading - User Class Example
summary: Backup slide showing operator overloading motivation with a User class. Comparing two Users with == requires an overloaded operator or getter methods.
main_text: C/C++ defines operators (+, *, -, ==, etc.) that work with basic data types like int, char, double, etc. C/C++ has no clue what classes we'll define and what those operators would mean for these 'yet-to-be-defined' classes. A User class example is shown with user.h: class User { public: User(string n); // Constructor. string get_name(); private: int id_; string name_; };. user.cpp: User::User(string n) { name_ = n; } string User::get_name() { return name_; }. user_test.cpp: User u1("Bill"), u2("Jane"); // Option 1: if(u1 == u2) cout << "Same"; // requires operator== overload. // Option 2: if(u1.get_name() == u2.get_name()) { cout << "Same" << endl; }. We can write custom functions to tell the compiler what to do when we use these operators!
notes_text: This backup slide presents the same concept as slide 4 but with a more practical User class example. Option 2 shows that without operator overloading, comparisons require calling getter methods, which is verbose. Operator overloading (Option 1) makes the code more readable and natural.
